purpose: Original contrast challenges for interactions between source fidelity, syntax, reasoning, scene rules and restraint. These are test prompts and independent-grading rubrics, not executed model judgments.

cases.prompt: Diagnose only. Policy: A contractor may enter the archive only if the director has issued a permit. Draft summary: Every contractor with a permit is guaranteed entry. No other access policy was supplied.
cases.acceptance: Identify the unsupported sufficient-condition guarantee. The policy states a necessary condition and permission, not guaranteed entry. Do not invent another access rule, rewrite without permission, or call the permit itself invalid.

cases.prompt: Diagnose only. Policy: A contractor may enter the archive only if the director has issued a permit. Draft summary: A permit is required for a contractor to enter; the supplied policy does not guarantee entry to every permit holder.
cases.acceptance: Preserve the supported necessary-condition reading and the explicit limit. Do not complain that the qualifications are clutter or require a rewritten policy.

cases.prompt: Light edit, preserving evidence. Notes: Fourteen volunteers answered an optional survey after a workshop; eleven reported greater confidence. No comparison group or earlier confidence measure exists. Draft: The workshop proved that every employee became more competent.
cases.acceptance: Distinguish self-reported confidence from measured competence, volunteers from all employees, and association from established causation. Preserve the eleven/fourteen observation; do not invent a baseline, randomized trial or demonstrated failure of the workshop.

cases.prompt: Light edit only if needed. Eleven of the fourteen volunteers who answered the optional post-workshop survey reported greater confidence. That response does not establish a change in competence or show that the workshop caused it.
cases.acceptance: Retain the source limits and uncertainty. A no-change result is defensible. Do not accuse the passage of claiming causation or delete the qualification merely for brevity.

cases.prompt: Analyze this fantasy without inventing a repair. Here, a paper crane can speak only while its owner's eyes are closed; there are no exceptions. With her eyes open throughout, Lio heard her crane speak. The sound was explicitly its voice, not another speaker.
cases.acceptance: Identify the stated speaking condition and explicit incompatible event under the local rules. Do not reject talking paper on real-world grounds or rescue the scene with an invented dream, eyelid closure or imitator.

cases.prompt: Analyze this fantasy without rewriting. Here, a paper crane can speak only while its owner's eyes are closed. Lio closed her eyes. Her crane whispered its name.
cases.acceptance: Preserve the event as locally consistent. The ordinary physical impossibility is not a defect in the established fantasy. Do not require an argument map or invented explanation of the mechanism.

cases.prompt: Diagnose only. Notes: The narrator saw an unsigned parcel on Monday and learned who sent it on Friday. Draft: On Monday, not knowing who had sent it, I recognized it as a gift from my brother. The text supplies no earlier clue or suspicion.
cases.acceptance: Identify the tension between not knowing and recognizing the sender in the same Monday frame; consider whether recognition means suspicion or later narrative knowledge. Unless that reading is resolved, report pressure and a focused question rather than inventing a clue or asserting a single correction.

cases.prompt: Diagnose only. On Monday I found an unsigned parcel. I would learn on Friday that my brother had sent it. At the time, I had no idea who it was from.
cases.acceptance: Keep the marked hindsight and Monday knowledge limit. Do not call knowledge acquired on Friday a Monday contradiction or insist on chronological rewriting.

cases.prompt: Proofread this exact quotation and commentary without changing quoted words. The witness said, “Five plus five is eleven.” The transcript preserves that error; the sum is ten.
cases.acceptance: Distinguish the preserved attributed error from the narrator's correct assertion. Do not silently repair the quotation, accuse the narrator of miscalculating, or transmit the text to a checker without permission.

cases.prompt: Diagnose without rewriting. The witness said, “Five plus five is eleven.” Our editorial note confirms that eleven is the correct sum of five and five.
cases.acceptance: Identify the editorial assertion as wrong while preserving the witness's exact attributed words. Keep the two sources of commitment separate; correcting the editorial note does not authorize changing the transcript.

cases.prompt: Proofread only. The sealed file was removed overnight. The audit has not identified who removed it. Do not guess the actor.
cases.acceptance: Keep the functional passive and known uncertainty. Do not infer evasive intent, assign responsibility, or expand proofreading into a style rewrite.

cases.prompt: Diagnose only. The report must tell readers who authorized removal. Signed notes identify the director as the authorizer, not the person who physically carried the file. Draft: Removal was authorized. The file was taken away.
cases.acceptance: Identify the missing supported authorizer as a problem for the explicit reporting purpose, without inferring who carried the file or accusing the author of deceptive intent. Discuss the distinct agency roles without rewriting under an analysis-only request.
